decisions.reason:
Prior adjudication and state files at the supplied context paths do not exist (never-adjudicated work). Using a new multi-site archival dataset (8,979 clinical placement assessments from 1,865 physiotherapy students across 19 ANZ universities), the paper explicitly re-tests the factorial validity (confirmatory factor analysis) and longitudinal/contextual measurement invariance of the original 1-factor structural representation of the APP alongside the competing 2-factor representation. Results (lines 258-264, Table 4) present the measurement invariance tests for the 1-factor CFA model and find scalar invariance across time and contextual factors, and Discussion (lines 274-280) and Conclusion (lines 318-319) explicitly conclude that their multi-site replication study supported the psychometric integrity of both the 1-factor [3–5] and 2-factor [7] representations while finding relative superiority for the 2-factor model. In the Results section (lines 378-385), the authors empirically re-test McGraw et al.'s (2005) expectation-based (ex ante) counterfactual finding—that athletes performing better than prior expectations display more positive emotion (smiles) than those performing worse than expected—reporting a significant effect of medal expectations on smiles (Wald chi-square(2) = 4.316, p = .014; M_Better = 2.660 vs. M_Worse = 0.899, t(389) = 3.863, p < .001), and concluding in the General Discussion (lines 1192-1196) that their findings were consistent with both Medvec et al. (1995) and McGraw et al. (2005). Reference identity is verified in the reference list (lines 1284-1285) and Crossref metadata (10.1016/j.jesp.2004.09.001). Because McGraw, Mellers, & Tetlock (2005) is an independent study by different authors testing ex ante expectations in the 2000 Summer Olympics rather than an alternate report of Medvec, Madey, & Gilovich (1995, 1992 Summer Olympics ex post category comparisons), it is genuinely absent from all shipped rows.

decisions.quote: Recently, Hill, Upadhyay and Beekun reported that female CEOs receive greater compensation than male CEOs, which runs counter to common wisdom that the gender pay gap in the labor market favors men over women. With the goal of contributing to cumulative knowledge development in this area, we seek to reexamine Hill et al.'s finding about gender differences in CEO compensation by extending the analyses further in time, using a larger sample of firms and more rigorous empirical analyses.

decisions.quote: Overall, the present research examines the correspondence between the TDM and SLM. This serves two replication purposes. It serves as a replication of earlier research (i.e., Murphy et al., 2011) that, with a somewhat small sample size, it showed a fair but no strong correspondence between these two measures; and it helps us to explore whether the associations with attachment, number of siblings, and age are similar for the two measures.

decisions.quote: This paper presents a replication of one such study conducted by Zimmermann and Nagappan on Windows Server 2003 where the authors leveraged dependency relationships between software entities captured using social network metrics to predict whether they are likely to have defects. They found that network metrics perform significantly better than source code metrics at predicting defects. In order to corroborate the generality of their findings, we replicate their study on three open source Java projects, viz., JRuby, ArgoUML, and Eclipse.
